title: Letters to his brother Quintus
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi058.perseus-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: quod autem me maxime movere solebat, cum audiebam illum plus apud te posse quam gravitas istius aetatis, imperi, prudentiae postularet quam multos enim mecum egisse putas ut se Statio commendarem, quam multa autem ipsum ἀφελῶσ mecum in sermone ita posuisse : 'id mihi non placuit ; monui, suasi, deterrui'! quibus in rebus etiam si fidelitas summa est, (quod prorsus credo quoniam tu ita iudicas), tamen species ipsa tam gratiosi liberti aut servi dignitatem habere nullam potest.
passages.english: But what used to trouble me most was when I heard that he had more influence with you than the dignity of your age, your command and your good sense demanded. For how many people do you think have urged me to recommend them to Statius? And how many things do you think he himself has said to me in conversation, quite artlessly, in this way: 'I did not approve of that; I warned, I advised, I dissuaded'! In these matters, even if his loyalty is complete (which I fully believe, since you judge it so), still the mere appearance of a freedman or slave with so much influence can carry no dignity.
passages.notes: The Greek ἀφελῶς ('artlessly, simply') is printed ἀφελῶσ in the edition, with a final sigma in the wrong form. The first sentence is grammatically incomplete in the Latin: the 'what' clause breaks off into the exclamations.

passages.original: nunc ea cognosce quae maxime exoptas. rem publicam funditus amisimus, adeo ut Cato, adulescens nullius consili sed tamen civis Romanus et Cato, vix vivus effugerit quod, cum Gabinium de ambitu vellet postulare neque praetores diebus aliquot adiri possent vel potestatem sui facerent, in contionem escendit et Pompeium 'privatum dictatorem' appellavit.
passages.english: Now learn what you most long to hear. We have lost the commonwealth utterly, so much so that Cato, a young man of no judgement but still a Roman citizen and a Cato, barely escaped with his life. He wanted to prosecute Gabinius for electoral bribery, and for several days the praetors could not be approached and would not grant him access. So he went up onto the platform at a public meeting and called Pompey a 'private dictator'.
passages.notes: This is C. Cato, the tribune, not M. Cato.

passages.original: itaque se comparat, homines ex agris accersit operas autem suas Clodius confirmat ; manus ad Quirinalia paratur. in eo multo sumus superiores ipsius copiis ; sed magna manus ex Piceno et Gallia exspectatur, ut etiam Catonis rogationibus de Milone et Lentulo resistamus.
passages.english: So he is getting ready and summoning men from the country districts, while Clodius is strengthening his gangs; a band is being prepared for the Quirinalia. In that respect we are much superior with his own forces; but a large band is expected from Picenum and Gaul, so that we may also resist Cato's bills concerning Milo and Lentulus.
passages.notes: 'His own forces' probably refers to Pompey's forces. 'Cato' here is C. Cato.

passages.original: in eius sermone ego utrumque soleo admirari, et te de suburbano emendo cum ad illum scribas non modo ad me non scribere sed etiam aliam in sententiam de suburbano scribere, et cum ad illum scribas nihil te recordari †de se de epistulis† illis quas in Tusculano eius tu mihi ostendisti, nihil de praeceptis Epicharmi : Γνῶθι πῶσ ἄλλῳ κέχρηται, totum denique vultum, sermonem, animum eius, quem ad modum conicio, †quasi† sed haec tu videris.
passages.english: In his conversation I regularly wonder at two things: that, when you write to him about buying a suburban property, you not only do not write to me but even write in a different sense about the property; and that, when you write to him, you remember nothing †about himself about those letters† which you showed me at his Tusculan villa, nothing of the precepts of Epicharmus, 'Know how he has treated another,' and in short [nothing of] his whole look, talk and mind, as I guess, †as if†. But you will see to that.
passages.notes: The text is corrupt at the two places marked with daggers in the edition; the sense there is uncertain. The Greek quotation means 'Know how he has dealt with another'.

passages.original: Salvius Ostiam vesperi navi profectus erat cum iis rebus quas tibi domo mitti volueras. eodem die Gabinium ad populum luculente calefecerat Memmius sic ut Calidio verbum facere pro eo non licuerit. postridie autem eius diei qui erat tum futurus, cum haec scribebam ante lucem, apud Catonem erat divinatio in Gabinium futura inter Memmium et Ti. Neronem et C. et L. Antonios M. f. putabamus fore ut Memmio daretur, etsi erat Neronis mira contentio. quid quaeris? probe premitur, nisi noster Pompeius dis hominibusque invitis negotium everterit.
passages.english: Salvius had set out for Ostia by ship in the evening with the things you had wanted sent to you from home. On the same day Memmius had roasted Gabinius splendidly before the people, so much so that Calidius was not allowed to say a word on his behalf. And on the day after that, which was still to come as I was writing this before dawn, a hearing to choose the prosecutor of Gabinius was to take place before Cato, between Memmius, Ti. Nero, and Gaius and Lucius Antonius, sons of Marcus. We thought it would be awarded to Memmius, although Nero was pressing his claim remarkably hard. In short? He is being pressed hard, unless our friend Pompey overturns the business against the will of gods and men.
passages.notes: The *divinatio* was the preliminary hearing to decide which of several applicants should be the prosecutor. The Cato here is the praetor M. Cato.

passages.original: quid plura de iudicibus? duo praetorii sederunt, Domitius Calvinus (is aperte absolvit ut omnes viderent) et Cato (is diribitis tabellis de circulo se subduxit et Pompeio primus nuntiavit). aiunt non nulli ut Sallustius me oportuisse accusare.
passages.english: What more about the jurors? Two ex-praetors sat on the jury: Domitius Calvinus, who voted openly for acquittal so that everyone could see, and Cato, who slipped away from the gathering once the ballots had been counted and was the first to bring the news to Pompey. Some people, Sallustius among them, say that I ought to have prosecuted.
passages.notes: Cato here is probably C. Cato. 'Diribitis tabellis' is rendered as 'once the ballots had been counted'; the verb strictly means sorting.

passages.original: Romae et maxime †et Appia ad Martis mira luvies †. Crassipedis ambulatio ablata, horti, tabernae plurimae ; magna vis aquae usque ad piscinam publicam. viget illud Homeri : ἤματ' ὀπωρινῷ, ὅτε λαβρότατον χέει ὕδωρ Ζεύς, ὅτε δή ῤ' ἄνδρεσσι κοτεσσάμενοσ χαλεπήνῃ.cadit enim in absolutionem Gabini : οἳ βίῃ εἰν ἀγορῇ σκολιὰσ κρίνωσι θέμιστας,ἐκ δὲ δίκην ἐλάσωσι, θεῶν ὄπιν οὐκ ἀλέγοντες.
passages.english: At Rome, and especially [on the] Appian Way near the temple of Mars, [there is] an extraordinary flood. Crassipes' promenade has been carried away, along with gardens and a great many shops; a great mass of water [reached] all the way to the public fish-pond. That line of Homer holds good: 'in the days of autumn, when Zeus pours down water most violently, when he is angry and enraged with men.' For it bears on Gabinius' acquittal: 'who by force in the assembly give crooked judgements and drive out justice, not heeding the regard of the gods.'
passages.notes: The text between the obelisks (†et Appia ad Martis mira luvies†) is corrupt. 'Luvies' is probably for 'eluvies' ('flood'). The Greek verses are Homer, Iliad 16.385–388, and the edition omits some lines.
